proof:
# Exact cap derivatives and depth-region section identities

Let S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) be nonempty, q=dim_H(S), and let
mu=H_q restricted to S. Put M=mu(S). These formulas are unnormalized;
divide all masses and cap derivatives by M for probability measure.

## 1. Intrinsic coarea, including all atomic boundary contributions

Only fibers of affine dimension q have positive H_q mass. For each
such index z write

    C_z=x_z+K_z, K_z subset V_z,

where V_z is a q-dimensional linear subspace of R^d and K_z is a
q-dimensional convex body in V_z. Write w_z=H_q(C_z).

Fix a nonzero ambient normal (a,b) and let

    F_(a,b)(s)=mu({(z,x):a dot z+b dot x>=s}).

On a fiber define b_z=proj_(V_z)b and c_z=a dot z+b dot x_z.
If b_z!=0, the push-forward of that fiber's q-volume under the displayed
linear functional has the Lebesgue density

    rho_z(s)=H_(q-1)({x in C_z:b dot x=s-a dot z})/|b_z|.       (1)

This is the ordinary coarea formula on the Euclidean affine space
x_z+V_z. Equivalently, rotate coordinates within V_z so its first
coordinate is b_z/|b_z| and apply Fubini. The denominator is the norm
of the continuous normal projected to the fiber's affine direction;
it is not the norm of the full ambient normal.

If b_z=0, the whole fiber is mapped to the single value c_z and the
push-forward is w_z delta_(c_z). Thus for q>=1 the exact push-forward
measure is

    nu_(a,b)=rho(s) ds+sum_(b_z=0) w_z delta_(c_z),
    rho(s)=sum_(b_z!=0) rho_z(s).                            (2)

All sums are finite. Formula (2) gives, for every s<t,

    F_(a,b)(s)-F_(a,b)(t)
      =integral_[s,t) rho(r)dr
         +sum_(b_z=0, s<=c_z<t) w_z.                       (3)

The half-open interval in (3) is dictated by use of closed upper
halfspaces: F(s)=nu([s,infinity)). In distributional notation
-dF=nu. At c_z a closed cap retains that fiber's mass and loses it
immediately to the right; replacing the cap by an open halfspace
changes the value there.

When q=0 all contributions are atoms, and (2)-(3) hold with rho=0.
No H_(-1) notation is used. When q=d and b!=0, all positive fibers
have V_z=R^d, so rho is simply the sum of the (d-1)-dimensional
section volumes divided by |b|, and F is absolutely continuous.
For a purely integer normal b=0 all cap changes are atomic.

For a moving boundary through y+t v with fixed normal (a,b), the
cap mass is F_(a,b)((a,b) dot y+t (a,b) dot v). Away from the listed
atomic levels, its derivative exists almost everywhere and equals

    -[(a,b) dot v] rho((a,b) dot y+t (a,b) dot v).             (4)

There is no justification for interchanging this derivative with an
infimum over normals or a maximum within a fiber without separate
regularity and optimizer hypotheses.

## 2. Convex depth regions and their projected depth profile

For 0<t<=1 define the normalized depth region

    D_t={y in conv(S):mu(H)>=tM for every closed H containing y}.

It is compact and convex. Convexity follows because a halfspace
containing a convex combination of two points contains at least one
of them, so depth at the combination is at least the smaller depth.
Closedness follows from upper semicontinuity of depth: for y_j ->y,
enlarge any containing closed halfspace by a threshold displacement
epsilon, include y_j eventually, then let epsilon decrease to zero.

Put g(z)=max_{x:(z,x) in conv(S)} depth(z,x), with g(z)=0 if the
fiber is empty. The maximum exists by compactness and upper
semicontinuity. For t>0,

    {z:g(z)>=t}=projection(D_t).                             (5)

Thus g has convex upper level sets, and is upper semicontinuous on
its compact projection domain. This is quasiconcavity, not concavity
of its values. Separate exact examples show that no fixed strictly
increasing transformation makes g concave on the real projection,
and that even log-concavity fails at integer midpoints.

## 3. Parallel section volumes do obey their ordinary BM inequality

For nonempty sections and 0<=lambda<=1, convexity gives

    (D_t)_( (1-lambda)u+lambda v )
      contains (1-lambda)(D_t)_u+lambda(D_t)_v.               (6)

Consequently, in the full-fiber-dimensional case d>=1,

    vol_d((D_t)_( (1-lambda)u+lambda v ))^(1/d)
      >=(1-lambda)vol_d((D_t)_u)^(1/d)
         +lambda vol_d((D_t)_v)^(1/d).                      (7)

The endpoints u,v must belong to the projection of D_t, so their
sections are nonempty. One endpoint may have zero d-volume. Extending
section volume by zero outside that projection does not make (7)
a global concavity assertion.

There is an intrinsic version. Let A=aff(D_t), let L=A-A, and put
V=L intersect ({0} x R^d), of dimension r. All sections lie in affine
cosets of this one fixed direction V. An affine right inverse to the
projection of A identifies the cosets by translations, preserving
their intrinsic Euclidean measures. Apply BM in V to (6). The function
H_r((D_t)_z)^(1/r) is concave on the projection when r>=1. If r=0,
each nonempty section is a singleton. This is entirely an ordinary
parallel-section theorem; it supplies no new lattice-point assertion.

There is also a critical-level detection issue. For the sharp example
C=[0,1] x [-1,1], the guaranteed level is t=1/4. On either integer
fiber z=0 or z=1, depth equals (1-|x|)/4: the own interval proves the
lower bound and an oblique cut isolates its smaller cap for the upper
bound. Thus both integer D_(1/4) sections are the singleton {0} and
have one-dimensional volume zero. For every t>1/4 they are empty,
with the same volume zero. Nevertheless D_(1/4) has nonempty ambient
interior, since its center (1/2,0) has depth 1/2 and every through-center
hyperplane is null, making depth continuous near that point. Therefore
even when the ordinary parallel-section BM theorem is nontrivial, its
integer section-volume values cannot distinguish the exact required
centers from absent fibers. Positivity of d-volume at the target level
would be a strictly stronger assertion than OC and is false here.

## 4. The three meanings of 'difference' behave differently

Define the fiberwise Minkowski difference, with nonempty operands, by

    E_z=C_z+(-(D_t)_z).

Its graph is convex: it is the linear image under (z,x,y)->(z,x-y)
of the convex fiber product {(z,x,y):(z,x) in C,(z,y) in D_t}.
Therefore its parallel section volumes have the same BM root-concavity
as in (7), on their common nonempty domain. Also, at a fixed z,

    vol_d(E_z)^(1/d)>=vol_d(C_z)^(1/d)+vol_d((D_t)_z)^(1/d).

If (D_t)_z is empty, its Minkowski sum with anything is empty. Filling
such a section by C_z is a new operation not covered by these statements.
Also E_z is a fiberwise construction, not the usual z-section of the
ambient Minkowski difference C-D_t, whose source indices can differ.

Neither the removed set C_z without (D_t)_z nor the erosion

    C_z minus_erosion (D_t)_z={v:v+(D_t)_z subset C_z}

has the same joint inclusion or root-concavity property. The companion
example `candidate ce5ad477e8315812` disproves it with
actual Tukey depth regions and positive-volume integer fibers.
